statement.quantifiers: For each fixed integer n>=1, then Y tends to infinity; X>=1 is fixed and nonintegral.
statement.convergence_class: The original term series converges in natural integer order for each fixed n, but is not absolutely convergent.

proof_obligations.derivation: A is the exact step cumulative sum. Stieltjes integration by parts on nonintegral endpoints gives the frozen finite identity with both boundary terms and signs exactly.
b_n'(t)=t^-2[P_n'(log t)-P_n(log t)]. For fixed n, P_n and P_n' are fixed polynomials, so |b_n'(t)|<=C_n(1+(log t)^(n-1))/t^2.
Bellotti Theorem 1.5 and (1.3)-(1.4) give |psi(x)-x|<=C x exp(-d(log x)^(3/5)/(log log x)^(1/5)) for large x. Since |floor(x)-x|<1, the frozen A bound follows.
For fixed n, |b_n(Y)|<=D_n(1+(log Y)^(n-1))/Y. The floor term vanishes, and polynomial(log Y) times exp(-d(log Y)^(3/5)/(log log Y)^(1/5)) tends to zero.
O2-O3 reduce the nontrivial term by u=log t to integral polynomial(u) exp(-d u^(3/5)/(log u)^(1/5))du, which converges because the stretched exponent dominates every constant multiple of log u.
Take Y->infinity in the exact finite identity only after O4-O5; the partial sums remain the original integer order with no permutation or regrouping.

Every 6k has prime divisors 2 and 3, so it is not a prime power and Lambda(6k)=0. For n=1 the harmonic subseries diverges. For n>=2 the leading Laguerre coefficient gives |P_n(log(6k))|>=c_n(log k)^(n-1) eventually, so the absolute subseries dominates c'_n sum (log k)^(n-1)/k and diverges.
